title: An LSM tree storage engine in Rust, built for a cache
summary: How CrowkisDB, a pure Rust LSM tree, stores an LLM cache: write-ahead log, MemTable, SSTables, Bloom filters, compaction, and the trade-offs.

body.text: An LSM tree storage engine in Rust is what sits under Crowkis. CrowkisDB writes every change to a write-ahead log, keeps recent data in an in-memory table, flushes it to sorted files on disk and merges those files in the background. It was written from scratch, with no RocksDB and no foreign-function calls, so the cache and its vector index run in one process.
What is an LSM tree?

A [log-structured merge-tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-structured_merge-tree) is a way to store key-value data that favours writes. It was described in 1996 by Patrick O'Neil and co-authors. Incoming writes are buffered in an in-memory component. When that buffer fills, it is written to disk in one sequential pass as an immutable sorted file. Nothing on disk is updated in place.

Reads pay for that. A lookup checks the in-memory component first and then the files on disk, newest first, because the newest file holds the latest value or deletion for a key. Two mechanisms keep reads affordable. Each file usually carries a Bloom filter that says when a key is definitely absent, so the file can be skipped. And a background process, compaction, merges files so there are fewer to check.

The durability comes from a [write-ahead log](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Write-ahead_logging): a change is recorded in the log, and the log reaches stable storage, before the change is applied anywhere else. After a crash the engine reads the log back and rebuilds what was in memory.

body.title: Write and read paths in an LSM tree storage engine
body.caption: A write goes to the log first, then to memory, and reaches a sorted file later. A read checks memory, then only the files whose Bloom filter cannot rule the key out.

body.text: What is inside CrowkisDB?
CrowkisDB is the engine under every Crowkis command. Its parts are the standard ones:

items: a **write-ahead log** (WAL) for durability
a **MemTable**, the in-memory table that holds recent writes
**SSTables**, the immutable sorted files a MemTable is flushed into
a **Bloom filter** per table, to skip files on reads
**compaction**, to merge tables in the background
a **manifest** that records which files make up the database
a bounded **block cache** for hot reads from disk
**snapshots** and archive rotation, for backups

body.text: It is pure Rust with zero FFI: no RocksDB, no LMDB, no sled. TTL expiry is part of the engine, and the [HNSW vector index](/blog/hnsw-explained-needle-in-a-million-haystacks/) that powers semantic lookup is kept by the same engine and persists with it.
How does a write reach disk?

items: A command such as `SET` or `CSET` arrives over RESP3 and is parsed by the server.
The handler passes it to a single-writer actor on a dedicated OS thread, through a bounded queue. When the queue is 90% full the server answers `BUSY` instead of queueing without limit.
The actor appends the change to the write-ahead log. By default it syncs the log to disk for every write before it acknowledges.
The change is applied to the MemTable, where reads can see it.
As in any LSM tree, a full MemTable is flushed to a new SSTable, and the manifest records the new file.
Compaction merges SSTables in the background.

body.text: One writer means every operation is atomic without locks between writers. Lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets and streams are stored as one blob per key, so an `LPUSH` or `HSET` is a single write through the same actor. The cost is that write throughput has one lane. That ceiling is known and tracked, and [the throughput ceiling](/blog/the-throughput-ceiling-we-wont-hide/) covers it.
Durability or throughput: what does the WAL setting change?

Syncing the log on every write is the slow, safe choice. Group commit is the fast one: writes are acknowledged from memory and the log is synced on a timer, so many writes share one sync. Crowkis exposes the choice as one variable, `CROWKIS_WAL_SYNC_INTERVAL_MS`, and measured both settings over the wire with a real server process.

What you risk

body.text: Both figures are from a development laptop, an Apple Silicon machine with 16 GB of RAM and 8 cores, with other builds running. Treat them as a floor and re-measure on your own hardware. The loss window at the grouped setting is 200 ms by construction, and it has not been tested under a real power cut.

For a cache the question is what a lost write costs. A lost cache entry is an answer you pay the model for again, which is cheap if it is one entry and less so if it is a burst. The default is the durable one, so the fast setting is something you opt into knowingly.
How do reads stay cheap?

A read checks the MemTable, then the SSTables. The Bloom filters do most of the work for keys that are not there. A [Bloom filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom_filter) is a small probabilistic structure that answers "possibly in set" or "definitely not in set": false positives are possible, false negatives are not. Wikipedia puts the size at fewer than 10 bits per element for a 1% false positive probability. A "definitely not" skips the file without touching the disk.
That matters more in a cache than in most stores, because a miss is normal traffic. Every new question is a miss on its way to the model, and it should not pay for a tour of the disk first.

For keys that are on disk, the block cache holds recently read blocks in memory. It is bounded by `CROWKIS_BLOCK_CACHE_BYTES`, and the process as a whole by `CROWKIS_MEMORY_LIMIT`. Under a container the engine reads the cgroup memory limit instead of total host memory, so that it refuses writes gracefully before the kernel kills it. A plain `GET` measured 103,000 ops/sec at 512 connections on the same laptop. That is a key read, and it says nothing about the semantic path, which is bound by embedding the query.
What happens on restart?

Opening the database replays the write-ahead log and loads the vector index. That can take a while with a large index, which is why the server binds its health-probe port before the database opens: `/readyz` answers 503 until the index is loaded, and `/livez` answers 200 so an orchestrator does not kill a process that is only warming up. [Deploying a self-hosted semantic cache](/blog/five-minute-deploy/) has the probe configuration.

On SIGTERM or SIGINT the server stops accepting connections and flushes the log before it exits, bounded by `CROWKIS_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS`, which defaults to 10000. There is one known gap. The background snapshot and compaction workers are not yet joined on shutdown, so a SIGTERM that lands while a snapshot is being published can force a full index rebuild on the next boot.
You can test the restart path yourself. Store an entry, restart the container, and read it back:

CSET "what is the capital of France" "Paris" TENANT smoke MODEL gpt-4o
# docker restart <container>, wait for /readyz to answer 200
CGET "what is the capital of France" TENANT smoke MODEL gpt-4o

body.text: The Crowkis build notes call this "the check that catches WAL bugs" and include it in the test of a locally built image. For backups, `CSAVE dest` writes a `.crowkbak` snapshot and replies only after it is synced to disk, and `CBGSAVE dest` does the same in the background.
Why not use RocksDB?

For most projects, RocksDB is the right answer. Its [own overview](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/RocksDB-Overview) describes a key-value storage library, forked from LevelDB, built from the same three constructs of memtable, sstfile and logfile. It has highly flexible configuration and three compaction styles: level, universal and FIFO. If your data fits a generic key-value engine, use one.
Owning the engine gives Crowkis three properties a borrowed one would not.

items: **One binary, one language.** RocksDB is a C++ library, so a Rust server reaches it through FFI. CrowkisDB has none, and the product ships as a single binary.

**The index and the store are one engine.** A semantic read is a vector search followed by checks on the candidates: tenant, model, TTL, confidence. With the HNSW index, the TTL logic and the key-value store in one engine, that sequence stays inside one process, and the index persists and recovers together with the data.

**A known workload.** A general engine exposes many settings because it serves every workload. A cache has a narrower one: entries that expire by TTL, and misses that must be cheap. The documented storage settings are few: the WAL sync interval, the block cache size, the memory limit and the connection limit.

body.text: Rust suits the request path. [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/) has no runtime and no garbage collector, so there are no collector pauses in the middle of a request, and memory safety is checked at compile time.
What did it cost, and what are the limits today?
Writing a storage engine means re-solving problems others solved long ago, and some are still open. These are the honest limits from the measured-capability notes:

items: **The soak test failed.** Under sustained concurrent writes and searches, the worst single request took 1,204 ms against a budget of 1,000 ms, at a corpus of 25,420 entries. The cause has not been isolated. No claim about tail latency under sustained write load stands until it passes.
**Writes have one lane.** The single-writer actor caps write throughput. Concurrent reads are the next infrastructure step.
**Every figure is from one laptop.** Nothing has been reproduced on server-class hardware or over hours of mixed load.
**The shutdown gap** described above can turn a badly timed stop into an index rebuild.

body.text: No garbage collector does not mean no stalls. The soak result shows that a background operation can still be felt by a request. If you are choosing an engine for your own product, the lesson is narrow: write your own only when the workload cannot be expressed in a generic one, and budget for the long tail of durability work. [How Crowkis earned production](/blog/how-crowkis-earned-production/) and [the correctness harness](/blog/84-of-84-correctness-under-fire/) show how that work is tested.
Common questions
Is CrowkisDB a fork of RocksDB or LevelDB?

No. It is written from scratch in Rust with zero FFI, and it does not embed RocksDB, LMDB or sled. It uses the same LSM design those engines made standard: a write-ahead log, a MemTable, SSTables, Bloom filters and compaction.
Does a cache need a durable storage engine?

An LLM cache does, more than a web cache. Each entry cost a model call to produce, so losing the cache on a restart means paying for those answers again. That is why the default syncs the log on every write.
What is group commit in a write-ahead log?

Group commit batches the disk sync for many writes into one. Crowkis does it on a timer set by `CROWKIS_WAL_SYNC_INTERVAL_MS`. Throughput rises sharply, and writes acknowledged since the last sync can be lost if the machine loses power.
Can I tune compaction in Crowkis?

The documentation lists no compaction settings. The storage settings it does document are the WAL sync interval, `CROWKIS_BLOCK_CACHE_BYTES`, `CROWKIS_MEMORY_LIMIT` and `CROWKIS_MAX_CONNECTIONS`. More engineering posts are under [engineering](/blog/topic/engineering/), and the product page is [Crowkis](/crowkis/).
